readerTitle: Why your co-founder's shares should arrive slowly
caseNote: 가상 기업 사례 (푸드트럭에서 시작한 식당, 일정 관리 앱) + 실제 관찰 (스타트업에서 흔한 4년 베스팅·1년 클리프 관행)
insight: 지분은 첫날 악수로 '받는' 것이 아니라 함께 일한 시간만큼 '버는' 것이어야 남는 사람과 회사를 지킬 수 있다.
misconception: 베스팅은 공동창업자를 못 믿을 때나 투자자가 요구할 때 쓰는 장치이고, 친한 사이라면 지분을 첫날 나눠 주면 된다.

sources.text: 스타트업 업계의 일반적 관행: 창업자·직원 지분에 4년 베스팅과 1년 클리프를 두는 구조 (예: Y Combinator 등 액셀러레이터의 창업자 가이드에서 흔히 설명됨)
푸드트럭·식당과 일정 관리 앱 사례 및 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: '4년 베스팅, 1년 클리프가 흔한 구조'라는 표현은 미국 스타트업 중심의 관행입니다. 나라와 업종에 따라 다를 수 있어 카드에는 'a common pattern in startups'로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 대표적 창업자 가이드 한 곳으로 표현을 확인하세요.
떠난 창업자의 미확정 지분 처리 방식(회사의 재매입권, 원래 가격 재매입 등)과 세금 처리는 나라마다 다릅니다. 법률·세무 조언이 되지 않도록 카드에는 '현지 변호사와 확인하라'는 수준으로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: Why your co-founder's shares should arrive slowly
body: Maya and Dan opened a taco truck as equal partners. They shook hands, split it 50/50 and signed the papers on day one.
Eight months later, Dan left for a steady job. Three years later, he still owned half of everything Maya built.

image.label: A taco truck with one partner working and one walking away
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 노란 푸드트럭 안에서 한 사람이 바쁘게 요리하고, 트럭 밖에서 다른 한 사람이 서류 가방을 들고 반대쪽으로 걸어감. 트럭 옆면에 반으로 나뉜 원형 지분 그래프. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: What goes in writing on day one?
body: You and a friend are starting a food truck together. You agree to split ownership 50/50. You both plan to work full time.
What do you put in the agreement?

options.text: Just the 50/50 split. We trust each other.
options.feedback: It keeps the friendship simple today. But if either of you leaves early, that person keeps half the business without doing half the work.

options.text: Each of us earns our half over four years. Leave early, keep only what you've earned.
options.feedback: It feels a little formal, but it protects whoever stays, and that could be either of you. This is the idea in this lesson.

options.text: We review hours each year and adjust the split to match.
options.feedback: It aims at fairness, but counting hours invites yearly arguments. Not all work is equal, and the split never feels settled.

cards.title: The partner who left still owned half.
body: Maya kept going. She ran the truck alone, then opened a small restaurant. Dan took half the profits and still had a vote on big decisions.
When Maya wanted to bring in a new partner chef, she had to give up shares from *her* half. The person doing the work owned less of it every year.
Nobody did anything dishonest. The agreement simply rewarded showing up on day one, not staying.

cards.title: Vesting
body: **Vesting** means you earn your shares over time instead of getting them all at once. If you leave early, you keep the part you've earned. The rest goes back to the company.
Many schedules add a **cliff**: a first stretch, often one year, where nothing is earned. Leave before it and you leave with nothing. Stay past it and a first block arrives at once.
With vesting, Dan would have kept little or nothing of his half.

cards.title: A four-year schedule with a one-year cliff
body: This is a common pattern in startups. Here it is for one founder's full stake.

breakdown.label: Months 0–11
breakdown.detail: Nothing earned yet. Leave now, keep nothing.

breakdown.label: Month 12: the cliff
breakdown.detail: A first quarter arrives at once

breakdown.label: Each month after
breakdown.detail: A little more is earned every month

cards.callout: Same split, but now it follows who stays.
cards.softwareNote: Investors in software startups often ask founders to put their own shares on a schedule like this. It shows the founders plan to stay and builds the same protection into the business.

cards.title: It isn't about distrust.
body: Vesting can feel like saying, *I think you'll quit.* It isn't. Both founders sign the same terms, so it protects whichever one stays.
People leave for good reasons too: illness, a family move, a burnout no one saw coming. Vesting turns a painful exit into a clear rule instead of a fight about who deserves what.
It also keeps shares free for the next person who joins and does the work.

cards.title: Vesting has gaps.
body: It doesn't fix a bad split. If the 50/50 was wrong, vesting just makes the wrong split arrive slowly.
A cliff can tempt someone to stay just past month 12, then leave. Some teams also agree what happens if a founder is pushed out, or if the business is sold early.
How unearned shares go back, and how they're taxed, depends on your country. Have a local lawyer write it up.

cards.title: Now it's a scheduling app.
body: Two founders each own 40% of a scheduling app for clinics. Both are on four-year vesting with a one-year cliff.
After 30 months, Priya leaves on good terms to care for a parent. She built the first version. How much should she keep?

options.text: All 40%. She built the first version.
options.feedback: It honors her early work, but the founder who stays carries the next years while Priya owns as much. It also leaves no shares for a replacement.
She keeps what she earned, and 15% goes back to the company. That's room to bring in someone to replace her work.

options.text: 10%, only what arrived at the cliff
options.feedback: It saves shares, but it ignores 18 months of work she was promised credit for. That breaks trust with everyone still on a schedule.

cards.title: Shares should be earned, not just handed out.
body: Split ownership on day one, but let each person earn it over time. Vesting protects whoever stays and the business itself.
**Try it today:** if you have partners, find your agreement. Write down what happens to each person's shares if they leave next month, next year and in three years.
